title: Real-World: Simple Calculator Parser
story: Someone types '5+3' into your calculator app. It's just text — but behind the scenes, your code must split it apart, identify the operator, convert both sides to numbers, and compute the answer — all without crashing on bad input.
why: Parsing an expression combines string manipulation, Result, and match — it's a microcosm of how interpreters and compilers work.
analogy: Parsing a math expression is like unpacking a flat-pack box — you find the instruction manual (the operator), separate the parts (left and right numbers), and assemble the result.
try_it: Extend the calculator to handle multiplication (*) and division (/). Use `find_operator` for each symbol. For division, check that the right operand is not zero before dividing — return Err("Division by zero") if it is. Test with "8*7" and "10/0".
tips: `string.str_slice(s, start, end)` extracts a portion of a string — use it to split at the operator position
Pass `string.str_length(expr)` as the end to slice to the end of the string
Search for operators left to right — the first operator found is the one you split on
common_mistakes: Slicing with wrong indices — `str_slice(s, 0, pos)` stops BEFORE pos, which is correct for getting the left side
Forgetting to skip the operator character when slicing the right side — start at `pos + 1`
Assuming the expression has exactly one operator — "1+2+3" finds the first '+' at position 1, treating it as "1" + "2+3"
